name: compound-components
intent: Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
problem: A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
context: Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
benefits: The call site composes the family declaratively (`<Select><Select.Option/></Select>`) and never threads the shared value or its callbacks through children.
One owner for the shared state: exclusivity, open/closed and validation invariants are enforced once in the parent instead of being re-derived by every child.
Children stay presentational, re-orderable and replaceable — adding, removing or interspersing children needs no change to the parent.
Encapsulation: the state shape is private to the family, so the parent can change internally without touching call sites, and consumers import one namespaced symbol instead of several coupled parts.
Cross-cutting behaviour — keyboard navigation, focus management, ARIA wiring, disabled propagation — is implemented once in the parent and applies to every child, including children added later.
State is implicit at the call site: consumers write declarative markup without knowing or caring about the wiring behind it.

The family can be extended with new child roles (a new TabPanel, a new MenuItem variant) without modifying the parent's internal child list — the open/closed principle is structural, not merely conventional.
tradeoffs: Implicit coupling: a child used outside its parent fails at runtime (missing context, missing group membership), never at compile time — no type system expresses 'must be a child of Select'.

The parent becomes a small framework: the hidden contract between parent and children must be versioned together, so any change to the published state has a blast radius across every call site that uses the family.

Ambient state costs renders: every consumer of the channel re-renders when the value changes, the clone-style form rebuilds elements and defeats memoization, and fine-grained updates need extra machinery (split channels, selectors, signals).
Debuggability and testing suffer: the state is invisible where it is used, so a child's behaviour can only be observed by rendering the whole family, and a child in isolation needs a fake parent.

Accessibility and form semantics become the implementer's job: replacing a native control means rebuilding roles, aria-expanded/aria-activedescendant, keyboard handling and form association — the classic failure mode of custom selects.

Only direct children of the parent receive the implicit channel by default — wrapping a child in an intermediate component (e.g. `
`) breaks the pattern unless Context API is used instead of clone-style injection.
Context API misuse (putting volatile or frequently-changing state in a single context value) causes widespread re-renders that are hard to diagnose and profile.

participants.responsibility: Owns the shared state and its invariants, publishes the value and update callbacks on the implicit channel, and renders the cooperating children inside that scope.

Declares its identity to the family (its value, order or content) and reads the published state instead of receiving it from the call site; renders only what its own contract allows and never mutates the state directly.
The value plus the update operations the parent publishes — a context value, a slot scope object, a group object, a cascading value, an environment key — the only channel between parent and children.
Composes the children and supplies local data (labels, items), but no shared state and no wiring; it decides the arrangement, the parent decides the behaviour.
Resolves the implicit channel down the tree and schedules re-rendering (context propagation, projection queries, environment stack, composition scopes, event re-dispatch).

use_cases: Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.

Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.

Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.

Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.
avoid_when: Two or three props on a single component cover the need (`<Select options={items}/>`): a hidden channel is more machinery than the API it replaces.
Children are arbitrary consumer content rather than cooperating parts (a Card or Layout that merely renders children) — pass props or a render function and skip the hidden contract.
The framework offers no implicit-injection channel (plain C, class-less templates, minimal Go UIs): the wiring degrades to manual registration, and explicit props or a builder function is simpler.

The native element already provides the semantics (form controls, details/summary, listbox): extending or styling the native control beats rebuilding its implicit contract and its accessibility layer.
The family would ship as a package consumed by other teams: a wide implicit contract needs documentation, versioning discipline and an upgrade path that a plain props API does not.
The widget is a one-off feature unlikely to be reused or extended — the added indirection cost exceeds the benefit for a single-use component.
anti_patterns: Module-level (singleton) shared state, so every instance of the widget on the page shares one selection; per-instance state is the parent's job.
Clone-style prop injection that silently overwrites props the call site already set (including the child's own callbacks), making child behaviour depend on invisible parent behaviour.
Children that render nothing or crash opaquely when used outside their parent, instead of failing with an explicit diagnostic message.
A monolithic parent with many boolean props that merely pretends to be compound — the parts cannot be re-ordered, replaced or used separately.
Children that reach into the parent's internals or the DOM to read the shared state instead of consuming the published channel.
A single 'god context' value that mixes unrelated pieces of state, causing every consumer to re-render on any change, even when they only depend on one slice.
design_principles: Encapsulation / information hiding: the state lives in the parent and is exposed only through the channel children need.
Single source of truth: exactly one owner for the shared value; children derive from it and never duplicate it.
Separation of concerns: composition (call site), behaviour and invariants (parent), presentation (children).
Fail fast at misuse boundaries: the implicit contract must be checked at runtime with a clear message, since types cannot express parent-child membership.
Open/closed: new children participate by declaring their identity, without edits to a hard-coded child list in the parent.
Context value stability: context values must be stable across renders (memoized) or every consumer re-renders — split contexts or use selectors to keep frequently-changing state isolated.
best_practices: Make the parent the only state owner and keep that state per instance; never close over module-level or global state.
Prefer the framework's injection channel (context, slots, environment, scope receiver, cascading value) over cloning elements: cloning breaks memoization, keys and refs.
Fail loudly when a child is used outside its parent — a hook or constructor check that throws with a diagnostic — rather than rendering a silent fallback.
Keep children presentational: they read the published value and call published callbacks, and never own or mutate the shared state.
Export the family as one namespaced symbol (Select.Option) so the intended composition is discoverable from a single import.
Pin the behaviour and accessibility contract (roles, aria-* attributes, keyboard handling, focus management) in the parent and test it there, not per child.
Document and version the hidden contract — which children are accepted, what each receives — because a parent/child version mismatch is a runtime failure.
Memoize context values passed to providers: extract objects outside the render function or use useMemo to prevent every consumer re-rendering on every parent render.
Split contexts for independent state slices when the widget has multiple orthogonal pieces of shared state (e.g. open/closed and selected value) — this limits the blast radius of re-renders.
Use TypeScript discriminated unions or branded types on context values to make the parent-child contract explicit and catch misuse at compile time in projects that use TypeScript.
Test the family as a contract: render the full family and assert the parent's behaviour, then test isolated children with a minimal test parent that provides the necessary context.
When using cloneElement-style injection, explicitly merge props rather than blindly spreading the cloned props last, which would overwrite the child's own caller-supplied handlers.
Provide a displayName on every child component so the React DevTools tree is readable — anonymous children make debugging the component hierarchy significantly harder.
sources: React community catalog: the Compound Components pattern popularized by Ryan Florence's Compound Components workshop/talk (React Training, 2017) and documented as the Compound Pattern in patterns.dev; catalog home: docs/design-patterns.md section 9, Client-side composition and reuse.
